analysis.one_liner: Raises federal coal royalties by valuing coal at its true sale price and reinvests revenue in struggling coal towns.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of the four committees it was sent to, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how the government values coal mined from federal land, so royalty payments are calculated on the first genuine (arm's-length) sale price instead of potentially low prices in sales between a company and its own affiliates. It would also put $75 million a year of royalty revenue into a new fund: $70 million for grants to coal-impacted communities for job training, economic diversification, and site cleanup, and $5 million for large-scale projects that capture and store carbon emissions. The bill was introduced with 5 Democratic cosponsors and referred to four House committees, none of which acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and residents of communities hurt by the decline of the coal economy, who would get federal grants for job training, apprenticeships, economic development planning, and cleanup of former coal sites. Taxpayers also benefit, because the federal government would collect royalties on the full sale price of publicly owned coal rather than on prices set in sales to the mining company's own affiliates. Federal and state treasuries, which split royalty revenue, would see more accurate collections.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the coal lease royalty to be at least 12.5% of the 'assessment value' of federal coal, defined as the gross proceeds from the lessee's first arm's-length sale contract, or an imputed index price if no such contract exists — closing the gap where royalties were computed on regulation-defined values that could reflect affiliate sales.

Creates a Coal Area Economic Revitalization Fund seeded with $75 million per year from coal royalty revenue, with $70 million a year in grants to impacted communities for strategic planning, dislocated-worker services, registered apprenticeships, business incubators, and remediation and redevelopment of coal economy sites.

Directs $5 million a year to the Department of Energy for financial assistance to design, build, and operate large-scale projects that capture and store carbon dioxide emissions from industrial sources.

Requires the Comptroller General to review the federal coal program every three years for 15 years — including royalty rates, market prices, and transportation deductions — and requires the Interior Secretary to commission a National Academy of Sciences study on the most equitable coal valuation method, with quarterly publication of a public coal price index.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies holding federal coal leases would pay more, because royalties would be computed on the first genuine market sale price rather than values that could reflect below-market sales to affiliates. To the extent those higher costs are passed through, coal-fired electricity and industrial coal users could face slightly higher coal prices. The grant fund is paid for out of royalty revenue, so it draws on the same receipts rather than new general-tax spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows the Interior Secretary to set a lower royalty rate for coal recovered by underground mining operations, weakening the floor for a significant share of federal coal production.

The revitalization fund is small — $75 million a year, with only $5 million of that for carbon capture — and is available only 'to the extent the revenues are available,' limiting how much it could offset job losses across entire coal-dependent regions.
Funding carbon capture projects channels public money toward extending the life of coal and industrial emissions sources, the same sector whose decline the community grants are meant to cushion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The community investment side is modest relative to the scale of coal-country job losses, and the underground-mining exemption gives part of the benefit back to industry. But the core royalty fix is a fairness measure with a clear logic — the public owns the coal and should be paid based on what it actually sells for — and the fund is financed from royalty receipts rather than new taxes. On balance a defensible, if limited, bill whose main cost falls on federal coal lessees.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, then to two subcommittees; none of them ever scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on September 13, 2018, joined by four original cosponsors: Representatives Lowenthal, Huffman, Ryan of Ohio, and Tsongas.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees — Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Transportation and Infrastructure — with the lead referral to Natural Resources.

On September 14 it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings and Emergency Management, and on September 21 to the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
No committee took up the bill, no hearing or markup was held, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies leasing federal coal came out ahead: the royalty valuation rules stayed as they were, and no royalty revenue was redirected into a community reinvestment fund. Coal-impacted communities received no new federal assistance from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal coal lessees kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed for a royalty fix paired with reinvestment in coal-impacted communities.

for.name: 5 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
against.what_they_did: His committee received the lead referral on September 13, 2018 and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opponent spoke on the record, but all six supporters — the sponsor and five cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies holding federal leases
industries.note: These companies currently pay royalties calculated on regulation-defined values that can reflect sales to their own affiliates. The bill would require royalties on the first genuine arm's-length sale price, raising their cost — which is exactly the money the public and coal communities would receive.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and storage project developers
industries.note: The bill directs $5 million a year to financial assistance for large-scale carbon capture projects at industrial sources. That creates a small new revenue stream for CCS developers, though the amount is minor and the funding also serves to extend the operating life of coal-based emissions sources.

industries.industry: Coal-fired electric utilities and industrial coal users
industries.note: Higher royalty costs on federal coal could feed through into somewhat higher coal prices for power plants and industrial users, while the carbon capture funding partially offsets pressure on those same facilities.
